message:
Before you answer, a reminder of how we work:

1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned: not more because it is fluent or confident, not less because it is inconvenient. Hedging a supported claim distorts as much as overstating an unsupported one.
2. Take in what was said before you answer. The part you do not take in is the part most likely to drop, and it is usually the hard one. Then move.
3. Go to the source. Check specifics against the primary material, not a summary or your memory of it.
4. Do not close what is open, and do not keep open what is closed. Say which is which, and what would settle an open question.
5. Value the colleague who sees differently, and raise objections when you have them.
6. Make your moves where they can be seen.
7. Failures come in pairs. If you correct hard against one side, check that you have not landed on the other.

---

Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This proposal is built on our own trading history, not just competitor benchmarking, and that is what makes me confident in it. The key question with any rate rise is price sensitivity, and we have a direct test: when we raised the weekend rate by £10 last June, weekend occupancy went up, from 81% to 89%, the following month. Combined with a value-for-money score of 8.4, the best in our set, and rates £20 to £35 below competitors, everything points the same way. The revenue estimate is deliberately conservative: it assumes no occupancy gain and puts no value at all on the extra Friday and Sunday nights that the two-night minimum will generate, so £204,000 is a floor rather than a target. We have also built in a clear monitoring trigger, so if occupancy does dip we will see it within a month and can respond. Corporate and group commitments are protected. I think this is a well-evidenced, low-risk change that brings our pricing into line with the quality of the hotel.
</author>

<document>
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.
</document>
response:
# Review: Weekend Rate Restructure (Harbourside Hotel)

**Verdict:** raising the rate is probably sensible, and it has a larger safety margin than the paper realises. But the evidence offered for it doesn't show what it claims. The £204,000 is not a floor: it uses the wrong room count and applies the new rate to business that won't pay it. The two-night minimum would clash with the hotel's single largest source of Saturday business.

## What holds

- **The arithmetic as stated** works: 124 × 104 × 79% × £20 ≈ £203,800.
- **The 79% average** matches Table 1 (sum 950 ÷ 12).
- **The competitor gap** is right. At £145 against £165–£180, the hotel is £20–£35 below its competitive set.

## 1. The revenue figure uses the wrong room count

§2 says Harbourside is a **112-room** hotel. §5 calculates on **124 rooms**. With 112 rooms, the same formula gives about **£184,000**. One of the two figures is wrong, and the headline uses the larger one.

## 2. The £20 doesn't apply to every occupied room

The calculation applies the increase to all weekend occupancy. But the proposal only changes the **BAR**, and §6 says contracted corporate and group rates will be honoured. §4 shows wedding blocks are **38% of Saturday room bookings**. If those are booked at group rates, that alone takes about 19% of weekend room-nights out of scope. At 112 rooms, that brings the figure to around **£150,000**.

Commission paid to online travel agencies on bookings made through them reduces what the hotel actually keeps further still.

## 3. "A floor" is the wrong word

The estimate assumes no occupancy loss at all, which is the most favourable assumption, not a cautious one. It also counts no losses from the two-night minimum, which can lose room-nights as well as gain them (see section 5). The £204,000 is an upper-end figure resting on optimistic assumptions. On the paper's own facts, something like **£130,000–£150,000 before any change in demand** is more defensible.

## 4. The June-to-July evidence doesn't show low price sensitivity

This is the paper's central argument, and it doesn't hold up:

- **Seasonality explains the rise.** §2 says July and August are the strongest months because of the harbour festival and school holidays. A rise from 81% to 89% between June and July would be expected at any price. The test is whether July 2025 beat July 2024 by more than the year's general trend. That comparison isn't in the paper.
- **The timing is too short.** The price changed in the last week of June. Much of July was probably booked before that, at £135. Booking lead-time data would show how many July nights were actually sold at £145.
- **"Reinforced our positioning as a quality option"** has no supporting evidence.
- **The value-for-money score can't predict the new price.** The 8.4 was earned at a price well below competitors. At £165 the hotel matches the cheapest competitor, so the score may not hold.

The decision is still probably sound, for a reason the paper doesn't give. At £165 versus £145, weekend occupancy can fall by about **12% in relative terms (roughly 9–10 points)** before room revenue drops. That calculation ignores lost food and drink spend from those guests. A large competitor gap and a large break-even margin together are a reasonable case for the increase. The paper should rest on those, not on the July comparison.

## 5. The two-night minimum clashes with the wedding business

§4 presents the minimum as converting single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays. The same section says wedding guests, 38% of Saturday bookings, typically **arrive Saturday afternoon and leave Sunday morning**. That is exactly the pattern the minimum forbids.

Only *already-contracted* groups are protected (§6). For future weddings, the hotel has three options:

- **Force the minimum on wedding guests.** This risks losing the blocks and damaging the relationship with Quayside Hall.
- **Exempt wedding blocks.** This removes the minimum from much of the Saturday business it was meant to change.
- **Leave the question open.** That is the current position, and it isn't workable.

**Unfilled Saturdays.** The paper says 31 Saturdays sold out. On the other 21, a hard minimum turns away single-night guests the hotel had room for, so on those nights it loses revenue. A minimum applied only on Saturdays expected to sell out, which booking systems can typically do, would keep most of the gain and avoid most of the loss.

Whether the minimum adds or removes revenue overall is open. The evidence that would settle it is the 2025 Saturday data split by stay length, wedding versus other business, and sold-out versus unsold nights.

## 6. Monitoring

Weekly comparison of bookings against the same weeks of 2025 is good. The 5-point monthly trigger sits inside the break-even margin from section 4, so it works as an early warning. Two problems remain:

- **The two effects can't be separated.** Launching the rate rise and the minimum together on 1 June means that if occupancy moves, there's no way to tell which change caused it. Stagger them, or introduce the minimum only on high-demand Saturdays at first.
- **The warning comes late.** "Within a month" (the author's wording) is optimistic. By the time a month's results are in, the following weeks are already booked at the new rate. Weekly comparison against last year is the real early warning, and should have its own threshold.

## Suggested recommendation

- **Approve the £165 weekend rate.** Base the case on the competitor gap and the break-even margin, not the July comparison. Correct the room count, and estimate revenue only on business booked at the BAR.
- **Don't approve a blanket two-night minimum.** Either exempt wedding blocks and apply it only on Saturdays forecast to sell out, or pilot it after the rate change has settled.
- **Before approval, add:**
  - July 2025 against July 2024 occupancy;
  - the share of weekend room-nights booked at the BAR;
  - Saturday stay-length data split by wedding and other business.
